title: Norway May Restrict Online Games for Under-16s
paragraphs: Norway is planning to stop children under the age of 16 from using social media, and the government now says that the restrictions may also include some online games and messaging apps.

In October 2026, the Norwegian government announced that it was finalizing the new law, which it plans to send to the country's parliament by the end of the year. The aim is to protect children from harmful content, addictive features, illegal advertising and unwanted contact from strangers.

At first, it was expected that online games and messaging apps would mostly not be affected by the law. However, the government has now decided to judge each platform based on the risks it poses to children. As a result, services such as TikTok, Snapchat and the online game platform Roblox are likely to be covered by the law. On the other hand, messaging apps that are used for communication with schools may still be allowed.

According to Lene Vågslid, Norway's minister for children and families, some platforms present themselves as games, but they are actually full of features such as recommendation algorithms and illegal advertising aimed at children. Vågslid said that children's safety must come first.
Under the proposed law, technology companies would be responsible for checking the ages of their users. Their systems would also have to follow European rules on data protection.
The plan has changed over time. A draft law in 2025 proposed a minimum age of 15, but in April 2026, the age was raised to 16.

Norway is not alone. Denmark has already adopted similar restrictions, and Spain is working on a ban for young people under 16. In France, an attempt to ban social media for children under 15 was blocked by the country's Constitutional Council because of concerns about freedom of expression. Meanwhile, in September 2026, the European Commission proposed a new law called the EU Kids Act, which would introduce age-based restrictions on social media, online games and other digital services.
The government did not explain how children's right to take part in online life would be protected under the new restrictions.
